an the Required Trust Amount. The Grantor\'s obligation to maintain the Trust Account at the Required Trust Amount is a continuing obligation and shall not be excused by any claim, dispute, or counterclaim asserted by the Grantor against the Beneficiary.

**Section 4.02 --- Annual Adjustment**

The Required Trust Amount shall be reviewed and, if necessary, adjusted on an annual basis, effective as of December 31 of each calendar year (each such date, an \"Adjustment Date\"). The annual adjustment shall be calculated by reference to the Beneficiary\'s most recent quarterly statutory financial statements filed with the Illinois Department of Insurance and shall take into account the Grantor\'s outstanding Reinsurance Obligations as of the Adjustment Date, including ceded outstanding loss reserves and ceded loss adjustment expense reserves as reported by the Beneficiary in its most recent quarterly or annual statutory financial statement. The Parties shall use commercially reasonable efforts to complete the annual adjustment calculation within sixty (60) days following each Adjustment Date.

Notwithstanding the foregoing:

> \(a\) The Required Trust Amount shall not at any time be reduced below the Minimum Trust Amount of Forty-Three Million Dollars (\$43,000,000), regardless of the level of outstanding Reinsurance Obligations; and
>
> \(b\) Any increase in the Required Trust Amount above the then-current Required Trust Amount shall be subject to the mutual written agreement of the Grantor and the Beneficiary. In the event that the Grantor and the Beneficiary cannot agree on an adjustment to the Required Trust Amount within sixty (60) days following an Adjustment Date, the Required Trust Amount shall remain at the level in effect immediately prior to such Adjustment Date, and either Party may invoke the dispute resolution provisions of Section 11.02 hereof to resolve the disagreement. Pending resolution of any such dispute, the Grantor shall continue to maintain the Trust Account at the then-current Required Trust Amount.

For purposes of this Section 4.02, the Beneficiary shall provide the Grantor and the Trustee with a written statement of the Grantor\'s outstanding Reinsurance Obligations as of each Adjustment Date, together with such supporting documentation as the Grantor may reasonably request.

**Section 4.03 --- Substitution of Assets**

The Grantor may, with Prior Written Notice to the Beneficiary and the Trustee, substitute one or more Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account with other Eligible Trust Assets of equal or greater fair market value, provided that: (a) the aggregate fair market value of the Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account after giving effect to such substitution is not less than the Required Trust Amount; and (b) the replacement assets satisfy all requirements for Eligible Trust Assets under this Agreement. The Trustee shall complete any requested substitution within three (3) Business Days following receipt of the Grantor\'s written substitution request and the deposit of the replacement assets. The release of the substituted assets to the Grantor shall occur simultaneously with the deposit of the replacement assets into the Trust Account on a \"delivery versus delivery\" basis, such that at no point during the substitution process does the aggregate fair market value of the Trust Account fall below the Required Trust Amount. The Grantor shall bear all costs and expenses associated with any substitution of assets.

**Section 4.04 --- Investment Income**

All Investment Income earned on the Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account, including without limitation interest, coupon payments, dividends, and realized capital gains, shall be credited to the Trust Account and shall form part of the Trust Fund. The Grantor shall be entitled to withdraw Investment Income from the Trust Account on a quarterly basis following each quarterly valuation date described in Section 4.01, provided that after giving effect to such withdrawal the aggregate fair market value of the Eligible Trust Assets remaining in the Trust Account is not less than the Required Trust Amount. The Grantor shall submit a written request to the Trustee specifying the amount of Investment Income to be withdrawn, together with a certification that the withdrawal will not reduce the Trust Account below the Required Trust Amount. Matured Assets shall be reinvested in Eligible Trust Assets in accordance with written instructions from the Grantor, subject to the requirements of this Agreement.

**[ARTICLE V --- WITHDRAWAL RIGHTS OF BENEFICIARY]{.underline}**

**Section 5.01 --- Right to Withdraw**

The Beneficiary shall have the right to withdraw assets from the Trust Account at any time and from time to time, without notice to or the consent of the Grantor, upon delivery of a Withdrawal Notice to the Trustee in substantially the form set forth in Exhibit A hereto. The Trustee shall distribute the requested assets or their cash equivalent to the Beneficiary within two (2) Business Days following receipt of a Withdrawal Notice that conforms on its face to the requirements of this Agreement. The Grantor expressly acknowledges and agrees that it shall have no right to object to, delay, condition, or prevent any withdrawal by the Beneficiary from the Trust Account. The Trustee shall not be required to notify the Grantor of any withdrawal prior to distributing assets to the Beneficiary, although the Trustee shall provide the Grantor with a copy of each Withdrawal Notice within three (3) Business Days following distribution.

**Section 5.02 --- Permitted Purposes for Withdrawal**

The Beneficiary may withdraw assets from the Trust Account for the following purposes, and for these purposes only:

> \(a\) to reimburse the Beneficiary for the Grantor\'s share of ceded losses and ceded allocated loss adjustment expenses paid by the Beneficiary under or in connection with policies reinsured pursuant to the Reinsurance Agreement;
>
> \(b\) to reimburse the Beneficiary for the Grantor\'s share of unearned premium reserves returned to policyholders upon cancellation, nonrenewal, or mid-term modification of policies reinsured pursuant to the Reinsurance Agreement;
>
> \(c\) to fund any balance due and owing from the Grantor to the Beneficiary under the Reinsurance Agreement that remains unpaid for a period of thirty (30) days or more after the date on which such balance became due and payable;
>
> \(d\) where the Reinsurance Agreement has been terminated, commuted, or has expired and is in run-off, to fund the Grantor\'s share of outstanding liabilities, including reserves for ceded losses, ceded allocated loss adjustment expenses, and ceded incurred but not reported losses;
>
> \(e\) to reimburse the Beneficiary for any other amounts recoverable by the Beneficiary from the Grantor under the terms of the Reinsurance Agreement, including without limitation amounts due upon commutation, interim or final settlements, or arbitration awards.

The Beneficiary shall certify in each Withdrawal Notice the amount of the withdrawal and the specific purpose or purposes thereof, by reference to one or more of the categories set forth in clauses (a) through (e) above. The Trustee shall be entitled to rely conclusively on the Beneficiary\'s certification and shall not be responsible for independently verifying the accuracy, propriety, or appropriateness of any Withdrawal Notice or the underlying transactions giving rise thereto. The Trustee shall have no duty of inquiry with respect to any Withdrawal Notice that conforms on its face to the requirements of this Agreement.

**Section 5.03 --- Priority of Beneficiary\'s Claims**

The assets held in the Trust Account shall be held for the sole and exclusive benefit of the Beneficiary and shall not be subject to any claims, liens, security interests, or encumbrances of any creditor of the Grantor (other than the Beneficiary) or any creditor of the Trustee. In the event of the insolvency, liquidation, receivership, rehabilitation, conservation, or similar proceeding involving the Grantor, the Beneficiary\'s right to the assets of the Trust Account shall have priority over all other claims against the Grantor with respect to such assets. No creditor of the Grantor shall have any right to attach, garnish, levy upon, or otherwise reach any assets held in the Trust Account, and the Grantor shall not pledge, hypothecate, or grant any security interest in the Trust Account or the assets held therein to any Person other than the Beneficiary.

**[ARTICLE VI --- DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF TRUSTEE]{.underline}**

**Section 6.01 --- Standard of Care**

The Trustee shall hold, manage, and administer the Trust Account in accordance with the terms and provisions of this Agreement, exercising the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims. The Trustee shall segregate the Trust Account and all assets held therein from its own assets and from any other accounts maintained by the Trustee. The Trustee shall maintain complete and accurate books and records with respect to the Trust Account, which books and records shall be available for inspection by the Grantor, the Beneficiary, or any applicable regulatory authority upon reasonable notice during normal business hours.

**Section 6.02 --- Trustee\'s Reporting Obligations**

The Trustee shall provide the following reports and statements to both the Grantor and the Beneficiary:

> \(a\) **Monthly Statements.** Within fifteen (15) Business Days following the end of each calendar month, the Trustee shall deliver a written statement listing: (i) all Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account as of the last Business Day of such month; (ii) the fair market value of each such asset; (iii) the aggregate fair market value of the Trust Account as of such date; (iv) all deposits to, withdrawals from, and other transactions affecting the Trust Account during such month, including the receipt of Investment Income and the maturity or redemption of assets; and (v) a statement confirming whether the aggregate fair market value of the Trust Account meets or exceeds the Required Trust Amount.
>
> \(b\) **Quarterly Certified Statements.** Within thirty (30) days following the last Business Day of each calendar quarter, the Trustee shall deliver a certified statement of the Trust Account\'s composition and aggregate fair market value, signed by a duly authorized officer of the Trustee. Such certified statement shall include a listing of all Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account by type, CUSIP number, par value, fair market value, and credit rating.
>
> \(c\) **Annual Audited Statements.** Within ninety (90) days following the end of each calendar year, the Trustee shall deliver an audited statement of the Trust Account prepared by an independent certified public accountant selected by the Trustee and reasonably acceptable to the Beneficiary. The cost of such audit shall be borne by the Grantor.

**Section 6.03 --- Trustee Compensation and Expenses**

The Trustee shall receive an annual fee equal to five one-hundredths of one percent (0.05%) of the average fair market value of the Trust Account during the preceding calendar year, payable quarterly in arrears. Based on the initial Required Trust Amount of Forty-Three Million Dollars (\$43,000,000), the estimated annual trustee fee would be approximately Twenty-One Thousand Five Hundred Dollars (\$21,500). In addition to the annual fee, all reasonable and documented out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Trustee in connection with the administration of the Trust Account (including reasonable legal fees and expenses, tax reporting costs, and custody charges) shall be reimbursed by the Grantor. All Trustee fees and expenses shall be paid from the Grantor\'s own funds and shall not be charged against or deducted from the Trust Account. In the event that the Grantor fails to pay any Trustee fees or expenses within thirty (30) days following delivery of the Trustee\'s invoice, the Beneficiary may, in its sole discretion, elect (but shall not be obligated) to pay such fees or expenses on the Grantor\'s behalf, and any amounts so paid by the Beneficiary shall constitute an additional Reinsurance Obligation of the Grantor to the Beneficiary.

**Section 6.04 --- Limitation of Trustee Liability**

The Trustee shall not be liable for any loss, diminution, or depreciation in the value of the Eligible Trust Assets held in the Trust Account arising from market fluctuations, changes in interest rates, the insolvency or default of any issuer of securities held in the Trust Account, or any other cause beyond the Trustee\'s reasonable control, provided the Trustee has acted in good faith and in accordance with the terms of this Agreement. The Trustee shall not be liable for any act or omission of the Grantor or the Beneficiary. The Trustee may rely conclusively on any written notice, instruction, certificate, or other communication it receives from the Grantor or the Beneficiary that the Trustee believes in good faith to be genuine and to have been delivered by a duly authorized representative of such Party. The Grantor and the Beneficiary shall jointly and severally indemnify and hold harmless the Trustee from and against any and all losses, liabilities, claims, damages, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees) arising out of or in connection with the Trustee\'s performance of its duties under this Agreement, except to the extent caused by the Trustee\'s own gross negligence, willful misconduct, or bad faith.

**Section 6.05 --- Resignation and Removal of Trustee**

The Trustee may resign at any time by giving not less than ninety (90) days\' prior written notice to both the Grantor and the Beneficiary. The Beneficiary may remove the Trustee at any time, with or without cause, by giving not less than sixty (60) days\' prior written notice to the Trustee and the Grantor. In the event of the Trustee\'s resignation or removal, a successor trustee shall be appointed by the mutual written agreement of the Grantor and the Beneficiary within thirty (30) days following the date of the notice of resignation or removal. If the Grantor and the Beneficiary fail to agree on a successor trustee within such thirty (30)-day period, the Beneficiary shall have the right to select the successor trustee in its sole discretion, provided that such successor trustee shall be a bank or trust company chartered under the laws of the United States or any state thereof, with trust assets under management of not less than Five Billion Dollars (\$5,000,000,000). The resigning or removed Trustee shall transfer all assets of the Trust Account to the successor trustee within ten (10) Business Days of the effective date of the resignation or removal, and shall provide the successor trustee with all books, records, and documentation relating to the Trust Account.

**[ARTICLE VII --- OFFSET RIGHTS]{.underline}**

**Section 7.01 --- Acknowledgment of Offset Rights**

The Parties acknowledge and agree that Article VIII of the Reinsurance Agreement grants each of the Grantor and the Beneficiary the right to offset any balance or amount owed by one party to the other under the Reinsurance Agreement against any balance or amount owed by the other party to the first party under any other reinsurance agreement between the Grantor and the Beneficiary, whether such other reinsurance agreement is currently in force, in run-off, or has been terminated (the \"Offset Rights\"). The Trust Account and the assets held therein shall be subject to such Offset Rights. Accordingly, to the extent the Grantor is entitled to exercise an Offset Right against amounts otherwise payable to the Beneficiary under the Reinsurance Agreement, the Required Trust Amount may be reduced by the amount of such offset, provided that the Grantor delivers to the Trustee and the Beneficiary a written Offset Notice in substantially the form set forth in Exhibit C hereto, specifying in reasonable detail: (a) the basis for the offset; (b) the reinsurance agreement(s) under which the offsetting balance or amount has arisen; (c) the amount of the offset; and (d) the resulting reduction, if any, in the Required Trust Amount. Upon receipt of an Offset Notice, the Trustee shall adjust the Required Trust Amount in accordance with the terms thereof, and the Grantor may withdraw from the Trust Account Eligible Trust Assets having a fair market value equal to the amount of the offset, provided that the remaining fair market value of the Trust Account shall not fall below the adjusted Required Trust Amount.

**Section 7.02 --- Survival of Offset Rights**

The Offset Rights described in Section 7.01 shall survive the termination, expiration, or commutation of the Reinsurance Agreement and shall continue to apply to the Trust Account for so long as any Reinsurance Obligations remain outstanding or any amounts remain held in the Trust Account. The Parties\' respective Offset Rights shall not be extinguished or impaired by the passage of time or the winding down of the Reinsurance Agreement or the Trust Account.

**[ARTICLE VIII --- TERMINATION OF TRUST]{.underline}**

**Section 8.01 --- Conditions for Termination**

This Agreement shall terminate and the Trust Account shall be closed upon the earliest to occur of the following:

> \(a\) the date on which the Grantor and the Beneficiary execute a written agreement to terminate this Agreement and close the Trust Account;
>
> \(b\) the date on which the Beneficiary delivers to the Trustee a written certification, signed by a duly authorized officer of the Beneficiary, stating that all Reinsurance Obligations of the Grantor under the Reinsurance Agreement have been fully and finally discharged and that no further amounts are or may become owed by the Grantor to the Beneficiary thereunder;
>
> \(c\) the date on which the Reinsurance Agreement is commuted in full in accordance with the commutation provisions thereof and all amounts due from the Grantor to the Beneficiary under the commutation have been paid in full and finally settled;
>
> \(d\) the date on which the Grantor becomes licensed or accredited as a reinsurer in the State of Illinois and the Beneficiary no longer requires the Trust Account to obtain credit for reinsurance on its statutory financial statements, provided that the Beneficiary has consented in writing to the termination of this Agreement on such basis; or
>
> \(e\) the date otherwise required by applicable law or regulation or by order of a court of competent jurisdiction.

**Section 8.02 --- Distribution of Trust Assets Upon Termination**

Upon termination of this Agreement in accordance with Section 8.01, the Trustee shall, within thirty (30) days following the effective date of termination, distribute all remaining assets in the Trust Account to the Grantor, net of: (a) any amounts owed to the Beneficiary under outstanding Withdrawal Notices that have been submitted but not yet processed; (b) any unpaid Trustee fees and expenses; and (c) any other amounts required to be withheld by applicable law. The Beneficiary shall have a period of thirty (30) days following receipt of notice of termination to submit any final Withdrawal Notices with respect to outstanding Reinsurance Obligations. The Trustee shall process all such final Withdrawal Notices prior to distributing any remaining assets to the Grantor.

**[I. Executive Summary]{.underline}**

Lakeshore Actuarial Group (\"Lakeshore\" or \"we\") was retained by Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company (\"Pinnacle\") to evaluate the projected profitability of a proposed 30% quota share reinsurance treaty (the \"Treaty\") with Argonaut Re Ltd. (\"Argonaut Re\"), a Bermuda-domiciled Class 3B reinsurer. The Treaty covers Pinnacle\'s commercial general liability (\"CGL\") book for the 2025 underwriting year (January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025), on a risks-attaching basis. Under the Treaty, Pinnacle cedes 30% of net premiums and 30% of net losses (including allocated loss adjustment expenses, or \"ALAE\") on subject business to Argonaut Re.

Based on Pinnacle\'s projected 2025 CGL net written premium of \$193 million, the estimated ceded premium under the Treaty is \$57.9 million. Argonaut Re\'s aggregate liability under the Treaty is capped at \$85 million per treaty year.

Our analysis models the sliding scale ceding commission and profit commission mechanics under three scenarios. The key findings are as follows:

> • **Base Case (expected loss ratio of 62.3%):** The Treaty is projected to be economically beneficial to Pinnacle, producing an adjusted ceding commission of 35.08% and meaningful loss ceding relief. No profit commission is payable under this scenario due to a modest deficit in the treaty account.
>
> • **Favorable Scenario (25th percentile loss ratio of 48.7%):** The Treaty is highly profitable for Pinnacle, with the ceding commission at the 38% maximum and a profit commission of approximately \$0.7 million.
>
> • **Adverse Scenario (95th percentile loss ratio of 81.4%):** Treaty economics deteriorate significantly. The ceding commission falls to the 28% minimum, no profit commission is payable, and Pinnacle\'s net cost of cession increases materially.

We note two important limitations of this analysis. First, the aggregate limit of \$85 million and its interaction with the sliding scale commission under extreme tail scenarios were not separately modeled in this analysis. If ceded losses were to approach or exhaust the aggregate limit, the combined effect of minimum commission and loss cap exhaustion would produce compounding adverse economics not captured in our scenario framework. Second, this analysis does not address statutory accounting treatment or risk transfer considerations under SSAP No. 62R (Property and Casualty Reinsurance). We recommend that Pinnacle management consult with legal counsel and statutory accounting advisors regarding credit-for-reinsurance and risk transfer compliance prior to execution of the Treaty.

**[II. Scope and Limitations]{.underline}**

**[Scope]{.underline}**

Lakeshore was retained by Pinnacle to perform the following:

1\. Project expected treaty-year loss ratios for the subject CGL book;

2\. Model the sliding scale ceding commission under base, favorable, and adverse scenarios;

3\. Model the profit commission calculation under each scenario; and

4\. Assess the overall economic impact of the Treaty on Pinnacle\'s CGL book.

**[Data Relied Upon]{.underline}**

In performing this analysis, we relied upon the following data and documents:

> • Pinnacle historical CGL loss experience (paid and incurred loss development triangles), accident years 2015 through 2024, as provided by Priya Ramanathan, Chief Actuary of Pinnacle, on November 18, 2024;
>
> • Pinnacle CGL earned premium and written premium by accident year, 2015 through 2024;
>
> • 2025 CGL net written premium projection of \$193 million, as provided by David Chen, CFO, on December 2, 2024;
>
> • Pinnacle CGL rate change history, 2015 through 2025 plan year;
>
> • Draft Quota Share Reinsurance Treaty dated December 18, 2024, as circulated by Whitmore Gallagher LLP; and
>
> • Argonaut Re financial summary provided by Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC (Catherine Voss, Managing Director).

**[Limitations]{.underline}**

The following limitations apply to this analysis:

1\. **No risk transfer analysis.** This analysis does not constitute a risk transfer analysis under SSAP No. 62R (Property and Casualty Reinsurance) or any other statutory accounting standard. Pinnacle should engage its statutory auditors or other qualified professionals to perform such analysis prior to executing the Treaty.

2\. **Aggregate limit and sliding scale modeled independently.** This analysis models the sliding scale ceding commission and the aggregate limit independently. Specifically, the adverse scenario models the effect of elevated loss ratios on the sliding scale commission but does not model the scenario in which ceded losses exhaust the \$85 million aggregate limit. If exhausted, the implied ceded loss ratio would be approximately 146.8% (\$85M ÷ \$57.9M). In such a scenario, the combined effect of the minimum ceding commission (28%) and aggregate limit exhaustion would create a compounding adverse impact on Pinnacle not captured herein. We recommend that Pinnacle model this interaction separately.

3\. **Inherent uncertainty.** Loss projections are inherently uncertain, particularly for long-tail CGL business involving products liability, construction defect, and completed operations exposures. Actual results may differ materially from the estimates presented.

4\. **Data not audited.** We have not audited or independently verified the data provided by Pinnacle. If such data is materially inaccurate, our conclusions could be significantly affected.

5\. **No legal opinion.** We have relied upon the treaty terms as provided and have not rendered any legal opinion regarding the Treaty\'s terms, enforceability, or regulatory compliance.

**[Actuarial Standards]{.underline}**

This analysis was performed in accordance with Actuarial Standards of Practice (\"ASOPs\") promulgated by the Actuarial Standards Board, including ASOP No. 36 (Statements of Actuarial Opinion Regarding Property/Casualty Loss and Loss Adjustment Expense Reserves) and ASOP No. 43 (Property/Casualty Unpaid Claim Estimates), to the extent applicable.

**[III. Background and Treaty Terms Summary]{.underline}**

**[III.A. Pinnacle CGL Book Overview]{.underline}**

Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company is an Illinois domestic stock insurance company (NAIC Code 24817), rated A- (Excellent) by A.M. Best Company with a Financial Size Category VIII designation. Pinnacle is licensed in 38 U.S. states and writes primarily commercial general liability, professional liability, and excess casualty lines.

For the calendar year ended December 31, 2024, Pinnacle reported direct written premium of approximately \$412 million across all lines, of which approximately \$187 million was attributable to the CGL book. Projected 2025 CGL net written premium is \$193 million, reflecting modest organic growth and rate increases.

Pinnacle\'s CGL book is composed of general commercial accounts (approximately 40%), contractors and construction (approximately 25%), products and completed operations (approximately 20%), and miscellaneous classes (approximately 15%). The products and construction segments exhibit long-tail development characteristics, with ultimate loss emergence extending well beyond ten years for certain claim categories.

Over the ten accident years 2015 through 2024, Pinnacle\'s CGL ultimate loss ratios have ranged from a low of 52.1% (accident year 2018) to a high of 71.8% (accident year 2020), with a ten-year weighted average of approximately 60.5%. Pinnacle\'s CGL policies generally carry per-occurrence limits in the range of \$1 million to \$5 million; policies with per-occurrence limits exceeding \$5 million are excluded from the subject business under the Treaty.

**[III.B. Summary of Treaty Terms]{.underline}**

The following summarizes the material terms of the proposed Treaty, based on the draft circulated by Whitmore Gallagher LLP on December 18, 2024:

**Parties:** Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company (cedant) and Argonaut Re Ltd. (reinsurer). The Treaty was placed through Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC.

**Type:** 30% quota share reinsurance.

**Term:** January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025 (risks-attaching basis).

**Cession:** 30% of net premiums; 30% of net losses including ALAE on subject business.

**Estimated Ceded Premium:** \$57.9 million (\$193M × 30%).

**Aggregate Limit:** \$85 million maximum liability of Argonaut Re per treaty year.

**Ceding Commission --- Sliding Scale:**

> • Provisional rate: 34% (corresponding to a 65% loss ratio midpoint)
>
> • Maximum: 38% (at loss ratio ≤ 55%)
>
> • Minimum: 28% (at loss ratio \> 75%)
>
> • Tier 1 (loss ratio 55.01%--65%): Commission slides from 38% to 34% at 0.4 percentage points per 1% increase in loss ratio
>
> • Tier 2 (loss ratio 65.01%--75%): Commission slides from 34% to 28% at 0.6 percentage points per 1% increase in loss ratio

**Profit Commission:** 15% of net treaty profit. Net treaty profit equals ceded premiums less ceded losses (including ALAE), less ceding commission, less a 5% overhead/margin allowance to Argonaut Re. Deficit carryforward applies for two consecutive years; deficits extinguish after two consecutive deficit years.

**Brokerage:** 2.0% of ceded premium payable by Argonaut Re to Baxter & Rowland (\$57.9M × 2.0% = \$1.158M). Pinnacle pays a separate \$125,000 annual advisory fee to Baxter & Rowland. Total intermediary compensation: \$1.283 million.

**Exclusions:** Asbestos and environmental pollution liabilities; cyber liability; professional liability (errors and omissions); nuclear, biological, chemical, and radiological exposures; and policies with per-occurrence limits exceeding \$5 million.

**Trust:** \$43.0 million trust at First Continental Trust Company, N.A., in New York, funded with U.S. Treasuries and investment-grade corporate bonds rated A- or better.

**Argonaut Re Profile:** Bermuda-domiciled; not licensed, accredited, or certified in any U.S. state; S&P rating BBB+; shareholder\'s equity \$340 million; 2024 net written premium \$520 million; combined ratio 98.2%.

**[IV. Methodology]{.underline}**

**[IV.A. Loss Ratio Projection Approach]{.underline}**

We projected ultimate loss ratios for the 2025 treaty year using a blend of three standard actuarial methods:

1\. **Paid Loss Development Method:** Chain-ladder development applied to paid losses by accident year, projected to ultimate using selected link ratios from Pinnacle\'s historical CGL 10×10 triangle (accident years 2015--2024).

2\. **Incurred Loss Development Method:** A similar chain-ladder approach applied to case incurred data (paid losses plus outstanding case reserves).

3\. **Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method:** An a priori expected loss ratio --- selected based on the weighted average of recent accident years, adjusted for cumulative rate changes and loss cost trends --- was blended with emerging actual development patterns. Heavier weight was placed on the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method for the most recent and least-developed accident years.

Selected ultimate loss ratios represent a weighted blend of all three methods. We applied an annual loss cost trend factor of 4.5% to adjust historical loss experience to the 2025 prospective level, and incorporated Pinnacle\'s cumulative rate changes over the projection period to restate historical loss ratios on a 2025 rate-level basis. All projected loss ratios include ALAE, consistent with the Treaty\'s definition of ceded losses.

**[IV.B. Scenario Selection]{.underline}**

We modeled three scenarios to capture a range of probable treaty outcomes:

1\. **Favorable Scenario (25th percentile):** Loss ratio of 48.7%, reflecting a benign loss environment, above-average rate adequacy, and favorable development on recent accident years.

2\. **Base Case (Expected/Mean):** Loss ratio of 62.3%, the central estimate of expected performance for the 2025 treaty year, consistent with Pinnacle\'s recent loss experience adjusted for trend and rate level.

3\. **Adverse Scenario (95th percentile):** Loss ratio of 81.4%, reflecting a severely adverse loss environment, including potential for large or catastrophic CGL losses such as mass tort events, large construction defect aggregations, or unexpected judicial expansions of CGL coverage.

The probability distribution underlying these scenarios was derived by bootstrapping residuals of the historical loss development triangles and fitting a lognormal distribution to ultimate loss ratio outcomes. The adverse scenario loss ratio of 81.4% reflects the 95th percentile of this loss ratio distribution prior to consideration of the aggregate limit. The aggregate limit is treated as a separate contractual feature not integrated into the scenario analysis.

**[IV.C. Commission and Profit Commission Modeling]{.underline}**

For each scenario, the adjusted ceding commission is calculated using the sliding scale formula:

> • If loss ratio ≤ 55%: Commission = 38.0% (maximum)
>
> • If 55% \< loss ratio ≤ 65%: Commission = 38% − \[(loss ratio − 55%) × 0.4\]
>
> • If 65% \< loss ratio ≤ 75%: Commission = 34% − \[(loss ratio − 65%) × 0.6\]
>
> • If loss ratio \> 75%: Commission = 28.0% (minimum)

The profit commission is calculated as 15% × max(0, Ceded Premium − Ceded Losses − Ceding Commission − 5% Overhead Margin). For this single-year treaty, the deficit carryforward mechanism is relevant only if the treaty is renewed; for purposes of this analysis, the profit commission is zero if the net treaty profit is negative.

**Important limitation:** The sliding scale and profit commission calculations are modeled against the full ceded loss amount implied by each scenario\'s loss ratio. The analysis does not cap ceded losses at the \$85 million aggregate limit. In reality, if ceded losses were to exceed \$85 million, Argonaut Re\'s liability would be capped, and losses above that threshold would revert entirely to Pinnacle\'s net retention. This cap is not reflected in the commission or profit commission calculations presented herein. We note this as a material limitation and recommend separate modeling.

**[V. Results]{.underline}**

**[V.A. Scenario Analysis --- Loss Ratios and Ceding Commission]{.underline}**

**Table 1: Treaty Loss Ratio and Sliding Scale Ceding Commission by Scenario**

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Scenario**            **Loss Ratio**   **Commission Tier**   **Calculation**                   **Adjusted Commission**
  ----------------------- ---------------- --------------------- --------------------------------- -------------------------
  Favorable (25th %ile)   48.7%            ≤ 55%                 Maximum applies                   38.0%

  Base Case (Expected)    62.3%            55.01%--65%           38% − (7.3 × 0.4) = 38% − 2.92%   35.08%

  Adverse (95th %ile)     81.4%            \> 75%                Minimum applies                   28.0%
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Under the base case, the 62.3% loss ratio falls 7.3 percentage points above the 55% threshold at which the commission begins to slide. Each percentage point above 55% reduces the commission by 0.4 percentage points: 7.3 × 0.4 = 2.92 percentage points. The adjusted commission is therefore 38.0% − 2.92% = 35.08%, which is above the provisional rate of 34% and favorable to Pinnacle.

Under the favorable scenario, the 48.7% loss ratio is below the 55% threshold, so the commission is at the 38% maximum. Under the adverse scenario, the 81.4% loss ratio exceeds 75%, so the commission is at the 28% minimum.

**[V.B. Scenario Analysis --- Treaty Economics (Detailed Dollar Projections)]{.underline}**

**Table 2: Treaty Economics by Scenario (\$ in millions)**

  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Item**                                **Favorable**     **Base Case**     **Adverse**
  --------------------------------------- ----------------- ----------------- -----------------
  Estimated Ceded Premium                 \$57.9            \$57.9            \$57.9

  Ceded Losses (LR × Ceded Premium)       \$28.2            \$36.1            \$47.1

  Ceding Commission (Rate × Ceded Prem)   \$22.0            \$20.3            \$16.2

  Overhead/Margin (5% × Ceded Prem)       \$2.9             \$2.9             \$2.9

  Net Treaty Profit / (Deficit)           \$4.8             (\$1.4)           (\$8.3)

  Profit Commission (15% of profit)       \$0.7             \$0.0             \$0.0
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Favorable Scenario.** Pinnacle receives \$22.0 million in ceding commission plus \$0.7 million in profit commission, totaling \$22.7 million in compensation on \$57.9 million of ceded premium, while transferring \$28.2 million in losses. The treaty is clearly beneficial to Pinnacle under this scenario.

**Base Case.** Pinnacle receives \$20.3 million in ceding commission, with no profit commission payable due to a modest \$1.4 million deficit in the treaty account. The adjusted commission of 35.08% exceeds the 34% provisional rate, which is a favorable outcome. Pinnacle cedes \$36.1 million of losses while retaining \$37.6 million in net premium after commission (\$57.9M − \$20.3M), and gains \$36.1 million of loss relief. The treaty is modestly beneficial.

**Adverse Scenario.** Pinnacle receives \$16.2 million in ceding commission at the 28% minimum, with no profit commission. The treaty still provides loss ceding relief --- \$47.1 million of ceded losses versus \$41.7 million of net premium retained after commission --- but the economics are significantly less favorable due to the reduced commission rate.

**Important caveat on the adverse scenario:** The 81.4% adverse loss ratio, applied to estimated ceded premium of \$57.9 million, produces estimated ceded losses of \$47.1 million, which is well below the \$85 million aggregate limit. Therefore, in this scenario, the aggregate limit is not breached. However, this analysis does not model more extreme tail scenarios (e.g., the 99th percentile or beyond) where ceded losses could approach or exceed \$85 million. If ceded losses reached \$85 million, the implied loss ratio would be approximately 146.8% (\$85M ÷ \$57.9M), the commission would remain at the 28% minimum, and all losses above \$85 million would be retained entirely by Pinnacle --- creating a compounding adverse effect (\"double penalty\") that falls outside the scope of this analysis.

**[V.C. Sensitivity Analysis --- Sliding Scale Commission]{.underline}**

**Table 3: Ceding Commission Sensitivity to Treaty Loss Ratio**

The last row (146.8%) is included for illustrative purposes only to show the loss ratio at which the \$85 million aggregate limit would be exhausted. At this point the commission is already at the 28% minimum, and Pinnacle would bear 100% of losses above \$85 million. This combined effect was not modeled in the scenario analysis presented in this report.

**[V.D. Profit Commission Analysis]{.underline}**

Under the favorable scenario, net treaty profit is approximately \$4.8 million, generating a profit commission of approximately \$0.7 million (15% × \$4.8M) payable to Pinnacle. Under the base case and adverse scenarios, the treaty is in a deficit position; no profit commission is payable.

The deficit carryforward mechanism provides that deficits carry forward for two consecutive years and then extinguish. For this single treaty year, the carryforward is relevant only if the treaty is renewed. If Pinnacle and Argonaut Re enter into subsequent treaties, the two-year extinguishment period means that a deficit from the 2025 treaty year would no longer burden the profit commission calculation after two consecutive years of deficits.

The combination of the profit commission structure --- which returns a share of favorable results to the cedant --- and the two-year deficit extinguishment --- which limits the period over which the reinsurer can recoup losses --- creates asymmetric economics that may warrant further analysis from a statutory accounting perspective. We have not performed a risk transfer analysis under SSAP No. 62R and express no opinion on whether the Treaty satisfies risk transfer requirements. The aggregate limit of \$85 million further caps the reinsurer\'s maximum loss exposure. Combined with the profit commission and deficit extinguishment, the aggregate limit narrows the range of outcomes borne by the reinsurer. We note these features without expressing an opinion on risk transfer compliance and recommend Pinnacle engage appropriate advisors to assess this question.

**[VI. Analysis of Key Economic Drivers]{.underline}**

**[VI.A. Loss Ratio as Primary Driver]{.underline}**

The Treaty\'s economics are primarily driven by the ultimate loss ratio on Pinnacle\'s 2025 CGL book. At the expected loss ratio of 62.3%, Pinnacle\'s adjusted ceding commission of 35.08% provides meaningful expense relief, covering a substantial portion of Pinnacle\'s acquisition and overhead costs attributable to the ceded portion of the book. The sliding scale structure creates alignment of interests: Pinnacle is incentivized to underwrite profitably because better loss experience increases the ceding commission toward the 38% maximum.

Notably, the steeper slope in Tier 2 (0.6 percentage points per point, compared to 0.4 percentage points per point in Tier 1) means that commission deterioration accelerates as the loss ratio worsens beyond 65%. This amplifies the economic impact on Pinnacle in adverse scenarios and provides an additional incentive for disciplined underwriting. Between a 65% and 75% loss ratio, the commission declines by a full 6 percentage points (from 34% to 28%), compared to only 4 percentage points of decline across the entire 55%--65% range.

**[VI.B. Impact of the Aggregate Limit]{.underline}**

The \$85 million aggregate limit represents approximately 146.8% of estimated ceded premium (\$85M ÷ \$57.9M). Under the base case (ceded losses of \$36.1M) and even the adverse scenario (ceded losses of \$47.1M), estimated ceded losses are well below the aggregate limit. However, extreme tail events --- such as a mass tort event, a series of large construction defect losses, or an unexpected judicial expansion of CGL coverage --- could theoretically drive ceded losses to approach or exceed \$85 million.

If ceded losses reach \$85 million, the following dynamics take effect: Argonaut Re\'s obligations are capped; Pinnacle retains 100% of all losses above \$85 million; the ceding commission is locked at the 28% minimum (since the loss ratio far exceeds 75%); no profit commission is payable; and the Treaty effectively provides no further risk transfer for losses above the aggregate limit. This creates a \"double penalty\" dynamic in which Pinnacle simultaneously receives reduced commission and retains uncapped losses.

Based on our loss distribution modeling, we estimate the probability of ceded losses exceeding \$85 million at less than 1%. We caution, however, that our distribution is fitted to historical data that may not fully capture emerging risks --- including mass tort exposure, social inflation, and nuclear verdicts --- that are particularly relevant to long-tail CGL business.

We recommend that Pinnacle consider modeling the aggregate limit exhaustion scenario in conjunction with the sliding scale commission to fully understand the tail risk retained. A dynamic financial analysis or stochastic simulation incorporating both features simultaneously would provide a more complete picture.

**[VI.C. Profit Commission and Deficit Dynamics]{.underline}**

The profit commission of 15% of net treaty profit, after the 5% overhead/margin allowance, provides Pinnacle with upside participation in favorable treaty performance. The 5% overhead/margin is a standard reinsurer load and reduces the available profit pool.

The two-year deficit carryforward with extinguishment is a cedant-favorable feature: it limits the period over which prior deficits can offset future profit commissions. In effect, after two consecutive years of deficits, the slate is wiped clean. For this single-year treaty, the deficit carryforward is relevant only if the treaty is renewed. From a structural perspective, the short extinguishment period, combined with the profit commission and aggregate limit, constrains the reinsurer\'s ability to recoup losses over time. This feature may be of interest to statutory accounting reviewers evaluating whether the Treaty satisfies SSAP No. 62R risk transfer requirements. We do not opine on this question.

**[VII. Comparison to Market Benchmarks]{.underline}**

The proposed Treaty terms are generally consistent with current market conditions for CGL quota share reinsurance. Quota share cession rates in the range of 20% to 40% are common for CGL books of Pinnacle\'s size, and the 30% cession rate falls within this typical range. Provisional ceding commissions in the range of 30% to 36% are market standard for sliding scale arrangements; Pinnacle\'s 34% provisional commission is within normal parameters. The 10-percentage-point spread between the minimum (28%) and maximum (38%) is moderately wide; some treaties employ narrower bands of 5 to 8 percentage points.

The 15% profit commission is at the market median, with the typical range being 10% to 20%. Aggregate limits are not universal on quota share treaties but are increasingly common; the \$85 million limit on approximately \$57.9 million of ceded premium (representing approximately 147% of ceded premium) provides meaningful capacity before exhaustion.

The brokerage fee of 2.0% of ceded premium payable by Argonaut Re to Baxter & Rowland is within the standard market range of 1.5% to 2.5%. The \$125,000 annual advisory fee payable by Pinnacle to Baxter & Rowland is a separate arrangement. Total intermediary compensation of \$1.283 million (approximately 2.22% of ceded premium) is reasonable and within market norms. The risks-attaching basis and quarterly bordereau reporting with 45-day lag are standard market features for treaties of this type.

**[VIII. Observations and Recommendations]{.underline}**

Based on our analysis, we offer the following observations and recommendations:

**1. Base case economics are favorable.** At the expected 62.3% loss ratio, the Treaty provides Pinnacle with an adjusted ceding commission of 35.08% --- above the provisional rate of 34% --- and meaningful loss ceding relief. The economics are within market norms and beneficial to Pinnacle.

**2. Adverse scenario economics are manageable but unfavorable.** At the 81.4% loss ratio (95th percentile), the commission drops to the 28% minimum and no profit commission is earned. The Treaty still provides loss ceding (\$47.1 million of losses transferred) but at significantly reduced commission terms.

**3. Aggregate limit and sliding scale interaction not modeled.** This analysis does not model scenarios in which ceded losses approach or exceed the \$85 million aggregate limit. Under such extreme scenarios, the combined effect of the minimum ceding commission and aggregate cap exhaustion would create compounding adverse economics for Pinnacle. We recommend that Pinnacle\'s risk management team perform stochastic modeling incorporating both the aggregate limit and the sliding scale commission simultaneously to quantify this tail risk. Specifically, a dynamic financial analysis simulating loss outcomes across the full distribution and applying both the commission sliding scale and the \$85 million cap at each simulation iteration would be appropriate.

**4. SSAP No. 62R risk transfer not assessed.** This report does not include an analysis of whether the Treaty satisfies risk transfer requirements under SSAP No. 62R. Several features of the Treaty --- including the aggregate limit (\$85 million), the profit commission with two-year deficit extinguishment, and the combination of these features with a relatively generous ceding commission structure --- may warrant scrutiny under the \"10-10 rule\" (i.e., whether there is at least a 10% probability of a 10% or greater present value loss to the reinsurer). We note that the aggregate limit caps the reinsurer\'s maximum loss at \$85 million, and the profit commission returns a portion of favorable results to the cedant, which in combination may narrow the reinsurer\'s expected net economic loss. We strongly recommend that Pinnacle retain a qualified actuary or accounting advisor to perform a formal SSAP No. 62R risk transfer test before executing the Treaty. Failure to satisfy risk transfer could result in the Treaty being accounted for as a deposit rather than reinsurance, which would eliminate the statutory surplus benefit of the cession.

**5. Adequacy of the provisional commission.** At the expected loss ratio of 62.3%, the adjusted commission of 35.08% slightly exceeds the provisional rate, suggesting the provisional rate is conservatively set and favorable to Pinnacle.

**Final Recommendation.** The proposed Treaty appears economically sound under the base case and favorable scenarios. The principal risks relate to extreme tail scenarios (aggregate limit exhaustion) and statutory accounting compliance (risk transfer), neither of which falls within the scope of this analysis. Pinnacle management should address these items prior to binding the Treaty.

**[IX. Reliances, Qualifications, and Actuarial Certification]{.underline}**

**[IX.A. Reliances]{.underline}**

In preparing this report, we relied upon the following data sources:

> • Pinnacle CGL paid and incurred loss development triangles, accident years 2015 through 2024, as provided by Priya Ramanathan on November 18, 2024;
>
> • Pinnacle CGL earned premium and written premium by accident year, 2015 through 2024;
>
> • 2025 CGL net written premium projection of \$193 million, as provided by David Chen, CFO, on December 2, 2024;
>
> • Rate change history for the Pinnacle CGL book, 2015 through 2025 plan year;
>
> • Draft Quota Share Reinsurance Treaty dated December 18, 2024, as circulated by Whitmore Gallagher LLP;
>
> • Argonaut Re financial summary provided by Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC (Catherine Voss, Managing Director).

We have not audited or independently verified the data provided by Pinnacle. If the data is materially inaccurate or incomplete, our conclusions could be significantly affected.

**[IX.B. Qualifications and Disclaimers]{.underline}**

This report is prepared solely for the use of Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company\'s management and its advisors. It is not intended for distribution to third parties without Lakeshore Actuarial Group\'s prior written consent.

The analysis is based on information available as of January 6, 2025. We note the following qualifications:

> • This report does not constitute a risk transfer analysis under SSAP No. 62R or any other statutory accounting standard.
>
> • This report does not model the interaction between the \$85 million aggregate limit and the sliding scale ceding commission under extreme tail scenarios.
>
> • This report does not address credit-for-reinsurance requirements, collateral adequacy, or regulatory compliance.
>
> • Actual results will vary, potentially materially, from the projections contained in this report.

**[IX.C. Actuarial Certification]{.underline}**

I, Daniel Horvath, am a Fellow of the Casualty Actuarial Society and a Member of the American Academy of Actuaries. I meet the qualification standards of the American Academy of Actuaries to render the actuarial opinions contained herein. This analysis has been prepared in accordance with applicable Actuarial Standards of Practice. To the best of my knowledge, this report is complete and accurate, subject to the reliances, limitations, and qualifications stated herein.

**[ARGONAUT RE LTD.]{.underline}**

**[2024 Financial Summary and Reinsurer Profile]{.underline}**

\ 

**Prepared by:** Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC (\"B&R\") 150 North Michigan Avenue, Suite 1200 Chicago, Illinois 60601

**Prepared for:** Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company 200 North LaSalle Street, Suite 2800 Chicago, Illinois 60601

Attention: David Chen, Chief Financial Officer

Scott Tillman, General Counsel

**Contact:** Catherine Voss, Managing Director Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC cvoss@baxterrowland.com \| (312) 555-7840

**Date of Report:** January 8, 2025

\ 

CONFIDENTIAL --- Prepared solely for the internal use of Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company in connection with the proposed 30% Quota Share Reinsurance Treaty with Argonaut Re Ltd. (Treaty Year: January 1, 2025 --- December 31, 2025). This document contains proprietary analysis and confidential financial information. Not for distribution to any third party without the prior written consent of Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC.

**[Section 1: Executive Summary]{.underline}**

Baxter & Rowland Intermediaries LLC (\"B&R\") has prepared this financial summary and reinsurer profile to assist Pinnacle Casualty Insurance Company (\"Pinnacle\") in evaluating the financial strength, creditworthiness, and regulatory standing of Argonaut Re Ltd. (\"Argonaut Re\") in connection with the proposed 30% quota share reinsurance treaty (the \"Treaty\") covering Pinnacle\'s commercial general liability (\"CGL\") book of business for the 2025 underwriting year (treaty period January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2025, risks attaching basis).

Argonaut Re is a Bermuda-domiciled Class 3B reinsurer, formed in 2019 and regulated by the Bermuda Monetary Authority (\"BMA\") under the Insurance Act 1978 and related regulations. Argonaut Re currently holds a financial strength rating of **BBB+ (Stable Outlook)** from S&P Global Ratings, most recently affirmed in the third quarter of 2024. Argonaut Re does not hold an A.M. Best rating.

It is important to note at the outset that Argonaut Re is **not licensed, accredited, or certified as a Certified Reinsurer in any U.S. state**, including the State of Illinois, where Pinnacle is domiciled and regulated by the Illinois Department of Insurance.

Key financial metrics as of December 31, 2024, based on Argonaut Re\'s audited financial statements, include total assets of approximately \$980 million, shareholder\'s equity of approximately \$340 million, 2024 net premiums written (\"NWP\") of approximately \$520 million, and a combined ratio of 98.2%.

The estimated ceded premium under the proposed Treaty is \$57.9 million, calculated as Pinnacle\'s projected 2025 CGL NWP of \$193 million multiplied by the 30% cession rate. The Treaty provides for an aggregate limit of \$85 million per treaty year. A trust agreement with First Continental Trust Company, N.A. in New York is contemplated to collateralize Argonaut Re\'s obligations under the Treaty, with a proposed initial trust fund amount of \$43.0 million.

Because Argonaut Re is unauthorized and non-certified in Illinois, Pinnacle\'s ability to take statutory credit for reinsurance ceded under the Treaty will depend on the adequacy of collateral arrangements as measured against the requirements of Illinois law. B&R\'s summary is provided for informational purposes only and does not constitute a legal opinion on the sufficiency of the proposed collateral arrangement for regulatory credit-for-reinsurance purposes. B&R recommends that Pinnacle consult with its outside legal counsel, Aldersgate & Harlow LLP, and its actuarial advisors, Lakeshore Actuarial Group, regarding credit-for-reinsurance requirements under Illinois law and the adequacy of the proposed trust fund to support full statutory credit.

**[Section 2: Company Overview and Corporate History]{.underline}**

**Full Legal Name:** Argonaut Re Ltd.

**Registered Address:** Victoria Place, 3rd Floor, 31 Victoria Street, Hamilton HM 10, Bermuda

**Domicile:** Bermuda

**Regulatory Classification:** Class 3B insurer under the Bermuda Insurance Act 1978

**Year of Formation:** 2019

**Key Officers:**

> • **Chief Executive Officer:** Henrik Jørgensen
>
> • **Chief Financial Officer:** Alastair McBride
>
> • **General Counsel:** Sophia Karides

Argonaut Re was established in 2019 as a multi-line reinsurer focused on property and casualty treaty reinsurance, with a particular strategic emphasis on North American casualty business. The company was founded with initial capitalization from a consortium of private equity sponsors and institutional investors, and it has since grown its capital base organically through retained earnings and selective capital contributions.

Since its formation, Argonaut Re has experienced significant premium growth. Net premiums written increased from approximately \$180 million in its first full year of operation (2020) to approximately \$520 million in 2024, representing a compound annual growth rate of approximately 30%. This growth trajectory reflects Argonaut Re\'s strategy of expanding its market presence across key lines of business during a period of generally favorable pricing conditions in the global reinsurance market.

Argonaut Re\'s principal lines of business include property catastrophe excess of loss reinsurance, casualty quota share and excess of loss reinsurance, and specialty lines reinsurance covering marine and aviation risks. Casualty business --- including general liability, professional liability, and umbrella/excess liability --- constitutes a significant and growing portion of Argonaut Re\'s overall premium portfolio. B&R understands that casualty lines represented approximately 55% of Argonaut Re\'s 2024 NWP.

Argonaut Re\'s legal counsel in the Treaty negotiation is Whitmore Gallagher LLP, Crawford House, 50 Cedar Avenue, Hamilton HM 11, Bermuda, with lead partner Thomas Ng.

**[Section 3: Regulatory Status]{.underline}**

**3.1 Bermuda Regulatory Status**

Argonaut Re is licensed as a Class 3B insurer by the Bermuda Monetary Authority (the \"BMA\"). The Class 3B designation reflects that Argonaut Re underwrites more than 50% of its net premiums from unrelated business (i.e., business sourced from cedants that are not affiliates of Argonaut Re) and is subject to the minimum capital and surplus requirements applicable to that class under Bermuda law.

Argonaut Re files annual statutory financial returns with the BMA in accordance with the Insurance Act 1978 and the Insurance Account Rules 2016. These filings include the Bermuda Solvency Capital Requirement (\"BSCR\") model, which calculates risk-based capital charges across Argonaut Re\'s assets, liabilities, and premium exposures. Argonaut Re is subject to the BMA\'s enhanced capital requirement (\"ECR\") framework, which establishes a minimum threshold for regulatory capital adequacy. B&R understands that Argonaut Re has reported compliance with the ECR and the target capital level (\"TCL\") in its most recent BMA filing for the year ended December 31, 2024.

The BMA has been recognized by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (\"NAIC\") as a Qualified Jurisdiction under the NAIC\'s Certified Reinsurer framework, meaning that Bermuda-domiciled reinsurers are eligible to apply for Certified Reinsurer status in U.S. states that have adopted the NAIC Credit for Reinsurance Model Law and Regulation. However, as discussed in Section 3.2 below, Argonaut Re has not applied for or obtained Certified Reinsurer status in any U.S. jurisdiction.

Argonaut Re does **not** prepare U.S. statutory financial statements and does not file with any U.S. state insurance department or with the NAIC.

**3.2 U.S. Regulatory Status**

**Argonaut Re is not licensed in any U.S. state. Argonaut Re is not accredited as a reinsurer in any U.S. state. Argonaut Re is not certified as a Certified Reinsurer in any U.S. state, including Illinois.**

This status has direct and material implications for Pinnacle\'s ability to take statutory credit for reinsurance ceded under the proposed Treaty. Under the NAIC Credit for Reinsurance Model Law, as adopted in Illinois under 215 ILCS 5/173.1 and corresponding Illinois Department of Insurance regulations, a ceding insurer may take credit for reinsurance ceded to an unauthorized, non-accredited, non-certified reinsurer only if the reinsurer posts collateral --- in the form of qualifying letters of credit, trust funds, or funds withheld --- sufficient to cover 100% of the ceding company\'s outstanding ceded liabilities. These liabilities include ceded unearned premium reserves, ceded outstanding loss and loss adjustment expense reserves, and ceded reserves for incurred but not reported losses (\"IBNR\").

Argonaut Re has not applied for Certified Reinsurer status in Illinois or any other U.S. jurisdiction. If Argonaut Re were to obtain Certified Reinsurer status, reduced collateral requirements might apply depending on the rating category assigned by the Illinois Department of Insurance. For example, a Certified Reinsurer in the highest-rated category (Secure-1) may be required to post collateral as low as 0% of ceded liabilities under certain state implementations. However, as of the date of this report, no such application has been filed by Argonaut Re, and B&R has no indication that Argonaut Re intends to pursue certification in the near term.

The proposed trust agreement between Argonaut Re and Pinnacle, to be held at First Continental Trust Company, N.A. in New York, contemplates an initial trust fund of \$43.0 million. The estimated annual ceded premium under the Treaty is \$57.9 million, and Pinnacle\'s total ceded liabilities --- including unearned premium reserves, outstanding ceded loss reserves, and ceded IBNR --- may exceed the \$43.0 million trust fund amount at various points during and after the treaty period.

B&R notes that the proposed trust fund amount of \$43.0 million represents approximately 74.3% of estimated annual ceded premium (\$43.0M / \$57.9M = 74.3%). **Pinnacle should confirm with its legal and regulatory advisors whether this collateral level is sufficient to permit full statutory credit for reinsurance under 215 ILCS 5/173.1 and the Illinois Department of Insurance\'s credit-for-reinsurance requirements for unauthorized, non-certified reinsurers.**

B&R further understands that the trust amount is subject to annual adjustment based on outstanding reserves but is not to fall below the \$43.0 million floor --- that is, the trust fund cannot be reduced below \$43.0 million regardless of adjustments. However, the trust agreement does not expressly tie the required funded amount to 100% of Pinnacle\'s actual outstanding ceded liabilities at any given time. The absence of such a linkage may create periods during which the trust fund is insufficient to cover the full amount of Pinnacle\'s ceded obligations.

**[Section 4: 2024 Audited Financial Summary]{.underline}**

**4.1 Balance Sheet (as of December 31, 2024)**

The following table presents a summary balance sheet for Argonaut Re as of December 31, 2024, derived from the company\'s audited financial statements prepared in accordance with Bermuda statutory accounting standards and audited by Thornhill & Marsh LLP, Hamilton, Bermuda. B&R has categorized certain line items for presentation purposes based on the audited financial statements.

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Line Item**                               **Amount (USD, millions)**
  ------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  **Assets**                                  

  Cash and invested assets                    \$710

  Reinsurance recoverables                    \$85

  Premiums receivable                         \$130

  Other assets                                \$55

  **Total Assets**                            **\$980**

  **Liabilities**                             

  Loss and loss adjustment expense reserves   \$380

  Unearned premium reserves                   \$175

  Other liabilities                           \$85

  **Total Liabilities**                       **\$640**

  **Shareholder\'s Equity**                   **\$340**
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cash and invested assets of approximately \$710 million represent the largest component of Argonaut Re\'s asset base, constituting approximately 72.4% of total assets. B&R understands that the investment portfolio is composed primarily of investment-grade fixed income securities, with an average credit quality of A and an average duration of approximately 3.5 years. Reinsurance recoverables of \$85 million represent amounts due from Argonaut Re\'s own retrocessionaires on business that Argonaut Re has ceded under its retrocession program.

Loss and loss adjustment expense reserves of \$380 million represent the largest liability on Argonaut Re\'s balance sheet. Of this amount, approximately \$120 million relates to outstanding loss reserves on long-tail casualty business assumed from various cedants. These long-tail casualty reserves cover general liability, professional liability, and excess casualty lines, where claims may take many years to fully develop and resolve. The \$120 million in long-tail casualty reserves represents a significant commitment on Argonaut Re\'s balance sheet, and long-tail casualty reserves are inherently subject to development uncertainty. Actual ultimate losses may exceed or fall below current reserve estimates, with potential implications for Argonaut Re\'s reported shareholder\'s equity and overall financial condition. This is relevant context for evaluating Argonaut Re\'s counterparty credit quality and the adequacy of the proposed \$43.0 million trust collateral arrangement.

It should be noted that these financial statements are prepared in accordance with Bermuda statutory accounting standards, which differ from U.S. statutory accounting principles (\"SAP\") and U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (\"GAAP\") in certain material respects, including the treatment of deferred acquisition costs, asset valuation, and reserve discounting. Pinnacle should be aware of these differences when comparing Argonaut Re\'s financial metrics to those of U.S.-domiciled reinsurers.

**4.2 Key Financial Ratios and Operating Performance**

The following table summarizes Argonaut Re\'s key financial ratios and operating results for the year ended December 31, 2024:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Metric**                          **2024 Value**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Net Premiums Written                \$520M

  Combined Ratio                      98.2%

  Loss Ratio (approx.)                64.5%

  Expense Ratio (approx.)             33.7%

  Net Income (approx.)                \$18M

  Return on Equity (approx.)          5.3%

  Premiums-to-Equity Ratio            1.53:1

  Reserve-to-Equity Ratio             1.12:1
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Combined Ratio.** The combined ratio of 98.2% indicates that Argonaut Re\'s underwriting operations are approximately breakeven on a calendar year basis. A combined ratio below 100% represents a marginal underwriting profit, while a ratio above 100% would indicate an underwriting loss. The 98.2% result suggests that Argonaut Re is generating a small underwriting profit, supplemented by investment income to produce overall positive net income.

**Loss and Expense Ratios.** The loss ratio of approximately 64.5% reflects net losses and loss adjustment expenses incurred relative to net premiums earned. The expense ratio of approximately 33.7% reflects underwriting expenses (including ceding commissions paid, brokerage, and internal operating costs) relative to net premiums written. The expense ratio is somewhat elevated for a reinsurer, which may reflect the cost of building out the company\'s operational infrastructure during its growth phase.

**Net Income and Return on Equity.** Net income of approximately \$18 million, combined with shareholder\'s equity of \$340 million, yields a return on equity of approximately 5.3%. This return is modest relative to the industry and reflects both the near-breakeven underwriting result and the contribution of investment income. Investment income contributed materially to overall profitability in 2024, although the precise allocation between underwriting income and investment income is not separately disclosed in the financial summary available to B&R.

**Premium Leverage.** The premiums-to-equity ratio of \$520 million to \$340 million, or approximately 1.53:1, is above the 1:1 benchmark that some rating agencies and market participants use as a general comfort level for reinsurers. While a ratio of 1.53:1 is within acceptable bounds and does not, by itself, indicate financial distress, it reflects a relatively leveraged balance sheet for a reinsurer of Argonaut Re\'s size and maturity. Given that Argonaut Re was formed only in 2019, the company\'s capital base has not yet had the benefit of extended periods of organic capital accumulation, and its premium volume has grown rapidly relative to its equity.

**Reserve Leverage.** The reserve-to-equity ratio of approximately 1.12:1 (\$380M / \$340M) provides additional context regarding balance sheet leverage. This ratio is within normal parameters for a property and casualty reinsurer but should be monitored in light of the \$120 million in long-tail casualty reserves noted in Section 4.1 above.
